items.html:
Concrete roads are extremely common in the Philippines.

NOTE: Thailand also has a lot of concrete roads.

The Philippines drives on the right.

NOTE: Within Southeast Asia, Cambodia, Laos, Taiwan and Vietnam also drive on the right.
Standard white licence plates with black text are used for passenger vehicles. You can also find many older plates from the 2002 series, which are recognisable due to their green tint.

Octagonal metal poles are quite common in the Philippines.

NOTE: They can sometimes be found in Bangladesh and some parts of Malaysia as well.
You will often see a single insulator at the top of a vertical bar which is attached to the side of a utility pole.

Middle road lines in the Philippines can be either yellow or white. In particular, you will often see combined yellow and white middle lines, which is not common in any other East Asian country.

Yellow road lines commonly have a distinct orange tint.
These tall, square yellow road stones are unique to the Philippines.
Chevrons are typically red on white.
Sign posts are often painted red, orange or yellow.
Tuk-tuks, also referred to as tricycles, are extremely common in the Philippines, in many areas they are more common than typical cars.
Although Filipino is the official language of the Philippines, English is extremely common to find on signs. It is the only major Southeast Asian country where you’re likely to come across English.

In Generation 3 you can come across a white Street View car with the black roof clearly visible.

You may also come across a silvery grey car, which is also found in Bhutan.

It is somewhat common to see grains being spread out on roads to dry.

NOTE: This practice is also common in Vietnam.

These black or white boxes are commonly seen on utility poles. Most of the time they feature a three letter abbreviation of the municipality you are in. The abbreviations will either have all three letters stand for the municipality, or the first two letters will abbreviate the municipality while the third letter indicates the province.

In the first image the "GMI" and "GMU" stands for the town of Gamu in the province of Isabela while the second image the "BGE" stands for the town of Bangued.

NOTE: Most towns do not have any standardised abbreviation so you might find many different abbreviations for the same place.

The Philippines have several different tuk-tuk and tricycle designs, roughly distributed as shown in this infographic.

_This image was provided by AeroGelo. You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Province names are very common to find on signs and can thus be very useful. However, they do not appear on the map, meaning they’re necessary to memorise in order to use them.

It is worth mentioning that Davao de Oro changed its name from Compostela Valley in 2019.
Landlines will start with a 0 followed by the area code. Mobile phone numbers start with 09.

Motorcycles in the Philippines have regional colour-coded plates as seen on this map. Notably, the northern half of the country has the coloured strip at the top, while the southern half has it on the bottom of the plate.

The forested mountain range in Northern Luzon is characterised by somewhat dry mountainsides and an abundance of pine trees. You may rarely come across a similar landscape on high-altitude roads in Mindanao.
While corn can be found in most of the country, it is most common on northern Luzon and on Mindanao.
The vast majority of Oil palm plantations are found on Mindanao.
The majority of sugarcane in the Philippines can be found on the islands of Negros and Panay.
Pineapple plantations are mostly found on Mindanao.

Banana plantations are almost exclusively found in central and southern Mindanao.

NOTE: Wild growing banana plants can be found all over the country, so make sure what you are seeing is an actual plantation before guessing.

Moluccan albizia are trees with light coloured trunks and pinnate leaves near the top of the tree. They are mainly found on Mindanao and are especially common in the eastern and central regions of the island.
Houses built with amakan walls, a traditionally woven bamboo mat, with a diamond pattern are almost exclusively found in the southern half of the country.

Houses built with amakan walls (referred to as Sawali in the north) with a diagonally woven pattern are mostly found on the island of Palawan, but can also be found throughout the northern half of the country.
In the Cordillera Administrative Region you can find yellow and black striped concrete guardrails.
White guardrails with three recurring black stripes are unique to the region of Bicol in southern Luzon.
Square concrete poles with an indent on both side, similar to the poles found in Chile, are mainly found north of Manila and in and around the city of Bacolod on the island of Negros.

A poletop made up of two tall vertical metal bars having an L-shaped cross-section which are connected via several thin wires, making it resemble a ladder, is unique to Manila and the surrounding area.

NOTE: You may sometimes come across similar looking poletops, with square bars instead of L-shaped ones, throughout the entire country. They will however almost never have more than two connecting wires.

Square metal mesh poles are found on Mindanao, mainly on the Zamboanga peninsula.

NOTE: Most of the poles found outside of the Zamboanga peninsula are found along highways and have poletops with three hanging insulators.
While most of the Philippines is strongly Christian, a region of western Mindanao is majority Muslim.
Decorations made of neon-green Mountain Dew bottles are commonly found in the north, particularly on northern Luzon.
This type of tractor, called a kuliglig, is mostly found on the plains around Cauayan on northern Luzon.
On central Bohol you can find these distinct round grassy hills. The hills generally have dark brown soil beneath the grass, earning them the name of Chocolate Hills.
The Arayat Volcano can be recognised by being completely surrounded by flat agricultural fields.
The Mayon Volcano is one of the tallest mountains in the Philippines and can be recognised by its almost perfect smooth cone shape. Beware that it will very often be covered in clouds.
In and around the city of Marawi, Mindanao you can find many destroyed houses and ruins from the Marawi siege in 2017.

These large decorated white waystones, commemorating the Bataan Death March, can be seen along roads going from Mariveles and Bagac in the south to San Fernando in the north.

NOTE: The Bataan Death March continued from San Fernando to Capas by train, where a larger memorial has been built.

The highway going south from Puerto Princesa on Palawan can be characterised by being very wide, often featuring six lanes, while simultaneously having very little traffic.

Along the road you will usually see this double electrical wire, which can help confirm your guess.
Lamp posts on Siquijor are typically painted yellow, with black stripes at the bottom.
Images and statues of ancient Roman soldiers can be found on the island of Marinduque.
You may find this black Street View car with a visible roof rack in and around the city of General Santos.
In northwestern Bohol you can find this Street View car with tape on the back.
An orange Street View car with visible side mirrors can be found on Corregidor Island.
This vehicle with several thick black bars can be found just south of the Mayon Volcano.

steps.title: Maps and resources
steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends the following maps instead:

  • A Balanced Philippines (map link) - 100k+ AI-generated locations.
  • Manananggal (map link) - 80k locations with greater representation of urban (without info), small islands, and unique areas.
  • Intersectionguessr - Philippines (map link) - 90k mostly pinpointable AI-generated locations.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise the Philippines:

  • Plonk It Philippines (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Philippines guide from step 2 to 3.

lm.name: Bicol Adidas Guardrails
lm.note: In an area including Bicol and Masbate, you will see guardrails marked with three black stripes. Careful: you can get more or fewer than three in other places as well, but if you see three, it is most likely going to be this area.

lm.note: The stems on which insulators sit at the top of poles is commonly encased in a plastic tube that makes it appear much thicker than usual on the island of Bohol.

lm.note: If a motorcycle plate has a colorful stripe on the bottom, you are in the bottom half of the country.

lm.name: Cotabato/Davao Umbrella Tuk-Tuk

lm.note: Tuk-Tuks with a crown roof can be found mostly in Northern Luzon. The crown consists of two separate parts, a "rectangular" part and a "crown-shaped" part. Some Tuk-Tuks elsewhere will have a wavy top, but are not made of two parts and thus are not crowns.

lm.note: Double pancake insulators are very rare, but most likely to be found along the coast of East Samar, from about the height of the island of Hilabaan all the way down to the southern tip.

lm.name: Flat Roof Tuk-Tuk
lm.note: Flat roofs are mostly found in the south. If it's a three-wheeler (as seen on the leftmost), you're probably on Mindanao.

lm.note: This cylinder with four distinct ridges is most common in Ilocos Norte, but can also be found in Biliran.

lm.note: Found in Western Visayas, these trikes feature a passenger compartment that resembles a spaceship, with a distinctly aerodynamic design.

lm.name: Bicol High-Roof Trike
lm.note: The standard Bicol high-roof trike features many large, squarish windows for both driver and passenger, a large connecting window between them, and additional windows on the sides and rear. The passenger side is open and spacious.

lm.name: Bicol Mid-Roof Trike
lm.note: The standard Bicol mid-roof trike shares many characteristics with the high-roof version: numerous large windows, a connecting window between driver and passenger, and a spacious passenger area.

lm.name: Bohol Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: Bohol trikes are large and boxy, with one large window and a crown. Their defining feature is an additional window located below the driver’s position.

lm.name: Bohol Flat-Roof Variation
lm.note: This tuk-tuk–style trike is exclusive to Bohol. It features small horn-like mirrors at the front and small side windows. From the back, it looks fairly generic but includes two rear windows.

lm.name: Bukidnon Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: Bukidnon trikes are long and distinctive, featuring a large square main window with two side windows next to it, forming a trifold layout. They often lean backward, usually have a crown on top, and may include side windows at the rear. These trikes are found in northern Mindanao and on Camiguin Island.

lm.name: Calabarzon trike
lm.note: This is the standard Calabarzon trike. Key features include the padded coverings above both the passenger and driver, the curved bar in front of the driver, and the shape of the passenger car with a belt running beneath the window. There are a few minor variations in shape (such as a window above the driver, below the passenger, or differences in car size), but most of these are not strongly regional within Calabarzon. I noticed that the majority of these trikes have a silver, mirror-like, metallic finish.

lm.name: Car-Looking Trike
lm.note: Very common in the Davao region and also frequent in Butuan City, these trikes resemble small cars in both shape and appearance. They are easy to recognize and come in a wide range of colors.

lm.name: Caraga High-Roof Trike
lm.note: Caraga trikes feature two distinct, squarish passenger windows, with a flat window beneath them. Several variations of this style exist.

lm.name: Catanduanes Mid-Roof Trike
lm.note: These trikes feature square, plane-like windows and a crown on the roof. Many variations can be found within the same area.

lm.name: Cebu High-Roof Pyramid Trike
lm.note: These trikes have a striking design, with a pyramid-like passenger compartment. In some cases, the window is divided into two sections.

lm.name: Cebu Umbrella
lm.note: On Cebu Island, some trikes feature a roof made from fabric or tissue-like material, resembling an umbrella. This style is extremely common across the island and can be found almost everywhere.

lm.name: Cotabato Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: Cotabato trikes sometimes have a number plate mounted on the roof. They feature one or two windows that slope slightly forward, while the body beneath the windows slopes backward. The flat roof also leans backward.

lm.name: Crown High-Roof Trike
lm.note: These high-roof trikes feature crowns above both the driver and passenger windows. If you see a high-roof trike with crowns, you are likely in the northern part of the country. The crown design is very distinctive, even across different body shapes.

lm.name: Davao Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: This is the typical Davao City trike. It features two large windows, a bar beneath the windows, a large flat roof, and windows that slope backward. Some versions include a crown or a protruding element at the bottom (more common in downtown Davao), but the overall shape is the defining characteristic.

lm.name: Davao Oriental Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: Along the Davao Oriental coast, trikes with flat roofs and windows divided into two sections are common. A large number plate is mounted beneath the windows, and the trikes are often brightly colored.

lm.name: Full leather back trike
lm.note: Similar to the leather-back trike, but with the difference that the leather also covers the roof. It can be found near Laoag City.

lm.name: General Santos High-Roof Trike
lm.note: This trike is unique to General Santos. The main window extends outward at an angle, the roof slopes forward, and the window often includes two or three horizontal lines. Beneath the main window are two small auxiliary windows. A specific shade of blue is common in downtown General Santos, while an orange variant is exclusive to Polomolok, just north of the city.

lm.name: Guimaras Low-Roof Trike
lm.note: On Guimaras Island, trikes tend to have rounded or aerodynamic shapes.

lm.name: Isabella Low roof
lm.note: The passenger side features a hexagonal-shaped window at the rear. This type of trike is common in the northern part of the country.

lm.name: Koronadal Low-Roof Trike
lm.note: These trikes feature a long, box-shaped low roof. A crown may appear on the passenger side, and a number plate is often visible beneath a small passenger window. They appear in various colors.

lm.name: Lanao Mid-Roof Trike
lm.note: Trikes near Lake Lanao feature a very specific vertical passenger window and vertical bars on the passenger side. The driver’s window is more horizontal or square-shaped, and the roof is black on both sides.

lm.name: Leather back Trike
lm.note: The leather-back trike can be found in the northern part of the country as well as in central Luzon, particularly in the Ilocos region. The back of the trike is easily recognizable by its black leather.

lm.name: Leyte Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: Trikes are far more common in Leyte than in Mindanao, where they tend to cluster around main roads. In Leyte, they are ubiquitous—even in rural areas. The standard Leyte trike features two slightly outward-tilting windows, a large curved crown on top, and a roof that slopes backward. The body shape beneath the windows is the easiest way to identify them

lm.name: Masbate Mid-Roof Trike
lm.note: This is the main Masbate trike design. The driver’s side is fully open with a roof, while the passenger side features a large window, a crown, metal bars, and a hexagonal shape. In Masbate City, these trikes are often yellow, though other colors exist across the region.

lm.name: Mindoro Low-Roof Trike
lm.note: All Mindoro trikes share a metallic design with vivid colors. Decorative metal bars are an integral part of their overall aesthetic.

lm.name: Misamis High-Roof Trike
lm.note: Common in northern Mindanao, these trikes feature airplane-style passenger windows. There are many variations, and they appear in a wide range of colors.

lm.name: Negros Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: These trikes feature a curved crown on top, two windows, and a large number displayed below the passenger window. They appear in many different colors.

lm.name: Negros Mid-Roof Trike
lm.note: In southern Negros, mid-roof trikes share the same retro, 1970s-inspired passenger compartment design. Some versions include an additional window on the roof.

lm.name: North Cebu High-Roof Trike
lm.note: These trikes are highly distinctive, with a passenger compartment shaped somewhat like a Japanese train car. They appear in various colors and are easy to spot across Cebu Island.

lm.name: North East Cebu High-Roof Trike
lm.note: Another Cebu variant features a small horizontal window in the passenger compartment.

lm.name: North Panay High-Roof Trike
lm.note: Here’s the northern Panay trike. He’s silly & boxy, and he’s a guy, and he’s a little short don’t make fun of him.

lm.name: Nueva Viscaya low roof
lm.note: The passenger side features a crown on the roof, and the trike is fitted with transparent plastic protection. These trikes are unique to this region

lm.name: Palawan Trikes
lm.note: Palawan trikes are among the most unique in the country. Their car-like shape reminiscent of a Smart car makes them immediately recognizable.

lm.name: Romblon High-Roof Trike
lm.note: If you encounter unusually shaped high-roof trikes, chances are you are in the Romblon region or on Sibuyan Island.

lm.name: Samar Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: Samar flat-roof trikes have a unique curved body shape that makes them easily recognizable. They are slightly wider than average and usually feature a black roof.

lm.name: Samar Mid Roof Trikes
lm.note: This type of trike that’s really small in size, has two large windows and a connecting window, and the passenger trike is very low are extremely common in Western Samar. This specific shade of red with these small details are common in Catbalogan City. These can also be identified by their silly looking singular window in the back.

lm.name: South Bukidnon Trike
lm.note: South Bukidnon trikes are generally green, with a single horizontal window and a flat roof. The roof is also green and often includes metallic crossbars.

lm.name: South Negros Flat Roof Trikes
lm.note: In southern Negros, trikes have a very distinctive design. The passenger compartment resembles a small 1970s-era car, often paired with a large square flat roof.

lm.name: South Panay Low/Mid-Roof Trike
lm.note: Southern Panay trikes feature a unique bumpy, curved body shape. The passenger window is a rounded square, and the driver’s side has no window.

lm.name: Sultan Kudarat Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: These trikes feature a large flat black roof, a small side window, and no lines on the main window. They are mainly found in Sultan Kudarat. Green versions with blue “POBLACION” text are specific to Isulan, while more colorful variants with numbers on the roof are unique to Tacurong City.

lm.name: Surigao del Norte Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: This downtown Surigao trike features an extremely long window with two or three horizontal lines, a small bumper beneath the window, and a rear bar with a side window. The roof slopes backward less than other styles, giving it a very distinct shape. These trikes appear in many different colors.

lm.name: Umbrella Trike
lm.note: Trikes with an umbrella-style roof can be found in the Zamboanga Peninsula and across Mindanao. These trikes are easily recognizable by their umbrella-shaped roofs. This type is common in Pagadian City and very common in Cotabato City.

lm.name: Zamboanga Flat-Roof Trike
lm.note: Zamboanga City has a wide variety of trikes, but this flat-roof model is distinctive. It often features a white line separating the passenger and driver sections, horizontally shaped windows, and elaborate decorations. Zamboanga trikes are especially known for their bright, colorful designs and ornamental details.

lm.name: Zamboanga High-Roof Trike
lm.note: This is essentially the only high-roof trike variant found throughout the Zamboanga Peninsula. The passenger window resembles an airplane window, the roof slopes backward, and the body slightly bulges beneath the window.

lm.name: Arayat Volcano
lm.note: The Arayat Volcano can be recognised by being completely surrounded by flat agricultural fields.

lm.name: Bohol Hills
lm.note: On central Bohol you can find these distinct round grassy hills. The hills generally have dark brown soil beneath the grass, earning them the name of Chocolate Hills.

lm.name: Mayon Volcano
lm.note: The Mayon Volcano is one of the tallest mountains in the Philippines and can be recognised by its almost perfect smooth cone shape. Beware that it will very often be covered in clouds.

lm.name: Northern Luzon
lm.note: The forested mountain range in Northern Luzon is characterised by somewhat dry mountainsides and an abundance of pine trees. You may rarely come across a similar landscape on high-altitude roads in Mindanao.

lm.name: South - Diamond Pattern
lm.note: • Houses built with amakan walls, a traditionally woven bamboo mat, with a diamond pattern are almost exclusively found in the southern half of the country.

lm.name: Chevrons
lm.note: • Chevrons are typically red on white.

lm.name: Marawi - Destroyed Houses
lm.note: • In and around the city of Marawi, Mindanao you can find many destroyed houses and ruins from the Marawi siege in 2017.

lm.name: Palawan - Diagonal Woven Pattern
lm.note: • Houses built with amakan walls (referred to as Sawali in the north) with a diagonally woven pattern are mostly found on the island of Palawan, but can also be found throughout the northern half of the country.

lm.name: Bicol Adidas guardrails
lm.note: In an area including Bicol, Catanduanes and Masbate, you will see guardrails marked with three black stripes. Careful: you can get more or fewer than three in other places as well, but if you see three, it is most likely going to be this area.

lm.name: Bohol thick insulator stem
lm.note: The stems on which insulators sit at the top of poles is commonly thick or encased in a plastic tube that makes it appear much thicker than usual on the island of Bohol.

lm.name: Davao Occidental quad pancake insulator
lm.note: If you see a quadruple pancake insulator on a pole top, you're going to be on the one road with coverage in Davao Occidental, along the coast, between approximately Don Marcelino and Bukid.

lm.name: East Samar double pancake insulator
lm.note: Double pancake insulators are very rare, but most likely to be found along the coast of East Samar, from about the height of the island of Hilabaan all the way down to the southern tip.

lm.name: Ilocos Norte and Biliran quad insulator
lm.note: This cylinder with four distinct ridges is most common in Ilocos Norte, but can also be found in southern Biliran.

lm.name: Manila and Ilocos Norte Star Wars insulator
lm.note: This type of insulator that looks like the buildings on Tatooine is most common in northern Luzon and in and around Manila.

lm.name: Manila sausage insulator
lm.note: This grey insulator with lots of small ridges that looks kind of solid is most common in and around Manila, but can rarely be found elsewhere.

lm.name: Mesh poles
lm.note: Flimsy mesh poles are common in the province of Zamboanga Sibugay. They also, rarely, appear in other provinces, but even then you should be on Mindanao.

lm.name: North Cebu yellow blocks
lm.note: In northern Cebu, you will find gray concrete guard blocks with their edges or sides painted yellow. These are not the only guard blocks in the area, so don't discount northern Cebu if you see, for example, fully yellow concrete blocks or walls and blocks with diagonal black and yellow stripes.

lm.name: North Luzon Chile poles
lm.note: Chile poles can be frequently found in northern Luzon, especially Cagayan, but careful - they can also appear, if less commonly, in northern Negros!

lm.name: Northwest Leyte and Biliran extender insulators
lm.note: Three ridges plus a long extender at the top to carry the wire are most commonly found in northwestern Leyte and northwestern Biliran.

lm.name: Palawan trike
lm.note: The trikes on the island of Palawan are recognizable by their single wide front window. Many of them look as if they were cosplaying as cars, with emblems and everything.

lm.name: Panay & Guimaras yellow backboards
lm.note: On the islands of Panay and Guimaras (the little island next to Iloilo), electricity counters are frequently mounted on yellow backboards. These can be horizontal or vertical, metal or wood.

lm.name: Quezon blue/red blocks
lm.note: In a small area on the isthmus of Quezon province, you will find alternating red and blue guard blocks.

lm.name: South Mindanao car
lm.note: In southern Mindanao, in the very South of the Philippines, there is some footage taken with a silver truck with a visible roof rack. Note that this is leftover, unculled old coverage that runs parallel to gen 4 images of the same locations, so you can still get the same roads with a different car.

lm.name: Southern Quezon acne blocks
lm.note: The southern peninsula of Quezon has these sloped concrete blocks with round spots made from small rocks that kind of look like a skin issue. Blocks in this style with straight edges are common throughout the country, and you can get slanted concrete blocks without the acne in other places as well, but the combination is exclusive to this area.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner
lm.name: Octagonal metal poles
lm.note:
Octagonal metal poles are quite common in the Philippines.

NOTE: They can sometimes be found in Bangladesh and some parts of Malaysia as well.

lm.name: Vehicle - Crown Roof Tuk-Tuk
lm.note: Tuk-Tuks with a crown roof can be found mostly in Northern Luzon. The crown consists of two separate parts, a "rectangular" part and a "crown-shaped" part. Some Tuk-Tuks elsewhere will have a wavy top, but are not made of two parts and thus are not crowns.

lm.name: Vehicle - Flat Roof Tuk-Tuk
lm.note: Flat roofs are mostly found in the south. If it's a three-wheeler (as seen on the leftmost), you're probably on Mindanao.

lm.name: Concrete roads
lm.note: If you're in Southeast Asia and see concrete roads, you're most likely in the Philippines, Thailand, or, much more rarely, Indonesia. If you're driving on the right side, it will be the Philippines, while driving on the left side indicates Thailand or Indonesia.

lm.name: Trikes/Tuk-Tuks
lm.note: Tuktuks and Trikes are an extremely common sight in the Philippines. In many areas, they are more common than cars.

lm.name: Yellow and white lines
lm.note: Center lines in the Philippines can be white or a (usually slightly orange-tinted) yellow. The combination of the two colors, which you can also often get, is not really a thing anywhere else in Southeast Asia and as such is a good indicator for the Philippines.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Middle road lines in the Philippines can be either yellow or white, they can also be full white.
  • In particular, you will often see combined yellow and white middle lines, which is not common in any other East Asian country.
  • Yellow road lines commonly have a distinct orange tint.

lm.name: chilie style pole
lm.note: Square concrete poles with an indent on both side, similar to the poles found in Chile, are mainly found north of Manila and in and around the city of Bacolod on the island of Negros.

lm.name: L-shaped cross section
lm.note:
A poletop made up of two tall vertical metal bars having an L-shaped cross-section which are connected via several thin wires, making it resemble a ladder, is unique to Manila and the surrounding area.

NOTE: You may sometimes come across similar looking poletops, with square bars instead of L-shaped ones, throughout the entire country. They will however almost never have more than two connecting wires.

lm.name: Octagonal metal poles
lm.note:
Octagonal metal poles are quite common in the Philippines.

NOTE: They can sometimes be found in Bangladesh and some parts of Malaysia as well.

lm.name: Square metal mesh poles
lm.note:
Square metal mesh poles are found on Mindanao, mainly on the Zamboanga peninsula.

NOTE: Most of the poles found outside of the Zamboanga peninsula are found along highways and have poletops with three hanging insulators.
